items.title: Web application engineering
items.bodyMarkdown: Build practical web engineering judgment through original lessons and real projects.
items.description: JavaScript, TypeScript, React, Node.js, and relational persistence.
targetOutcomes: Build, debug, test, and maintain a web application.

items.title: The web development workflow
items.bodyMarkdown: Trace a request, make focused changes, and debug from evidence.

items.title: Follow a browser request
items.bodyMarkdown:
A support agent clicks a ticket in the browser. The screen changes, but the ticket may have come from a different computer. Understanding that boundary makes debugging much less mysterious.

The browser is the **client**. It presents controls, gathers input, and sends a request. The server receives the request, applies rules, and returns a response. A database is a separate store used by the server; the browser should not receive its credentials.

An HTTP request describes an operation with a method, a path, headers, and sometimes a body. For example, GET /api/tickets/42 asks for a representation of ticket 42. The path identifies the resource; it is not the response data. A response includes a status code, headers, and a body. A 200 response might contain JSON describing the ticket. The browser parses that JSON and renders a component. A 404 response says the resource is unavailable under the API’s policy.

Think of the round trip as a sequence of observable boundaries: a click handler runs; a request leaves the browser; a route matches; the server checks access and reads data; a response arrives; the client updates the display. Each boundary gives you a place to collect evidence. The browser’s Network panel shows the request and response even when the screen itself looks wrong.

The server owns authoritative rules such as access control and persistence. A disabled button improves the experience, but somebody can send a request without that button. The browser owns presentation and immediate feedback. Both sides may validate a title: the browser to help the agent quickly, and the server to protect the stored data.

A successful network request does not prove the UI is correct. If the response contains a title but the page is blank, inspect parsing, state updates, and rendering next. If no request appears, inspect the interaction and client code before changing a database query.
objectives: Identify request and response fields.
Separate presentation from authoritative server decisions.
items.workedExampleMarkdown:
~~~http
GET /api/tickets/42 HTTP/1.1
Accept: application/json

HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Content-Type: application/json

{"id":"42","title":"Printer offline"}
~~~

The request asks for ticket 42. The response status reports success; the final JSON object is the response body. The React component decides how to display its title.
commonMistakes: Calling the request path the response body.
Treating client-side hiding as an authorization check.
Assuming a blank screen always means the server failed.
items.summary: Inspect each boundary separately: input, request, server decision, response, and rendering.

items.title: Use Git and project commands
items.bodyMarkdown:
A ticket feature is ready to save, but your working folder contains both the intended change and an unrelated experiment. Git helps you make the boundary of that change explicit.

Your working tree contains the files you are editing. The staging area describes what the next commit will contain. A commit records that staged snapshot with a message. Saving in an editor does not automatically stage or commit a file. A remote repository is another copy of the history; committing locally does not publish it.

Start with git status to see the working tree and staging state. Read git diff to inspect unstaged changes. Stage only the relevant files, then read git diff --staged before committing. That final review catches debug output, accidental edits, and secrets before they become part of a snapshot. A useful commit message describes the behavior changed, such as “Reject blank ticket titles.”

Project commands are another boundary worth reading. A package.json scripts entry maps a friendly name to an actual command. Running pnpm test only works if the project defines a test script, and the meaning of that script belongs to that repository. A missing-script error is different from a test assertion failure. The first means the command was not configured; the second means the test runner started and observed unexpected behavior.

Use the package manager and lockfile already in the repository. A lockfile records resolved dependency versions so another installation can reproduce them. Avoid switching managers casually or editing a lockfile by hand. Read the README, inspect scripts, install dependencies with the documented command, and run baseline checks before changing code.

When a command fails, preserve its output and exit status. “It did not work” is too broad to guide a repair. “The test script invokes vitest, but that executable is missing after installation failed” identifies a specific dependency problem. A failing baseline is a setup issue to resolve before you interpret the deliberately failing mission tests.
objectives: Distinguish working, staged, and committed changes.
Diagnose a package script failure from its output.
items.workedExampleMarkdown:
~~~sh
git status --short
git diff
git add src/tickets.ts tests/tickets.test.ts
git diff --staged
git commit -m "Reject blank ticket titles"
~~~

Stage a focused change only after inspecting it. The staged diff is what the commit records. A separate push is needed to send the commit to a remote.
commonMistakes: Assuming git add commits a file.
Staging every changed file without inspecting unrelated work.
Treating “missing script” as a failed test assertion.
items.summary: Inspect the working diff, stage the intended change, inspect the staged diff, and then commit. Read project scripts before running them.

items.title: Debug from evidence
items.bodyMarkdown:
A support ticket page crashes only when its optional assignee is missing. A productive investigation starts with what you can observe, not with the first plausible code change.

A stack trace identifies where an error was thrown and the chain of calls that led there. Start with the error message and the first frame in your own code. A library frame may explain the mechanism, but it often is not where your application made the invalid assumption. The trace gives you a location to inspect; it does not establish the original cause by itself.

Reproduce the problem with known inputs. Record what you did, what you expected, and what actually happened. Then reduce the example while preserving the failure. If a hundred-ticket fixture fails, try one unassigned ticket. If a full page crashes, test the formatter that reads assignee.name. A minimal reproduction makes the hypothesis cheaper to test and easier to explain to somebody else.

Choose a hypothesis that can be contradicted by evidence: “The formatter assumes assignee is always present.” Inspect the input at the failing boundary, or add a focused test using an unassigned ticket. If the test fails with the same error, you have strengthened the connection between the assumption and the defect. If it does not, check whether the reproduction omitted an important condition.

Fix the boundary where the assumption is made. If unassigned tickets are valid, represent that state explicitly and return an appropriate label. Do not swallow every exception in the page and pretend rendering succeeded. A broad catch may hide the evidence and leave the user looking at stale data.

After the repair, test both the failing case and a normal assigned ticket. A regression test should fail with the original implementation and pass after the fix. That property is more useful than merely increasing the count of tests. Finally, remove temporary logs that contain personal data and leave a concise explanation of the defect and the evidence that confirmed it.
objectives: Read a stack trace to locate an application assumption.
Design a minimal reproduction and a regression case.
items.workedExampleMarkdown:
~~~text
TypeError: Cannot read properties of null (reading 'name')
  at assigneeLabel (src/ticket-view.ts:12:28)
  at renderTicket (src/ticket-view.ts:34:9)
~~~

Inspect the input passed to assigneeLabel. A fixture with assignee: null is a smaller reproduction than the entire dashboard. Test a null assignee and an assigned ticket before considering the repair complete.
commonMistakes: Changing several unrelated components before reproducing the failure.
Assuming the top library stack frame is the root cause.
Catching and ignoring every error instead of handling the supported empty state.
items.summary: Use a reproducible observation, a falsifiable hypothesis, a small test, and a repair at the failing boundary.

items.title: JavaScript values and control flow
items.bodyMarkdown: Make conversion, boundaries, and side effects explicit.

items.title: Make conversions explicit
items.bodyMarkdown:
A ticket-import form gives you a retry count as text. The string "0" and the number 0 look similar on screen, but they behave differently in a program. A reliable boundary makes that difference explicit before business logic uses the value.

JavaScript values have types. Strings represent text, numbers represent numeric values, and booleans represent true or false. null is an intentional absence marker; undefined often means a value was not supplied. An object groups named values. The typeof operator is useful for inspecting input, with historical exceptions such as typeof null returning "object".

Strict equality, written ===, compares without converting between these types. Therefore "0" === 0 is false. Loose equality, written ==, can convert operands, which makes apparently simple comparisons depend on extra rules. Prefer a clear conversion step followed by strict comparisons when reading an external value.

Number(text) converts numeric text, but conversion is not validation by itself. An empty string and a whitespace-only string both convert to zero. A nonnumeric string becomes NaN, which represents an invalid numeric result. Number.isFinite checks whether a value is a finite number without converting a string for you. Number.isInteger additionally checks for a whole number. The input policy must say whether negatives, fractions, exponent notation, and surrounding whitespace are allowed.

A truthiness check asks whether a value behaves as true in a condition. It does not ask whether the value is present or valid. Numeric zero, an empty string, null, and undefined are falsy, while the string "0" is truthy. Thus if (!count) rejects a legitimate count of zero. Use a check that expresses the actual rule, such as count === null for your chosen absence marker.

For the practice converter, accept nonempty strings that convert to finite nonnegative integers. Reject blank input before conversion. Return null when input is invalid; return a number otherwise. This gives callers one unambiguous result shape. Test a valid zero separately from blank text, because combining those cases would hide the most important boundary.
objectives: Predict strict equality and explicit numeric conversion.
Separate a missing value from a valid zero.
commonMistakes: Using truthiness to reject a valid zero.
Assuming Number always returns a valid number.
Treating conversion as a complete input policy.
items.summary: Validate the input policy explicitly, convert once, and compare values of the intended type.

items.title: Put boundaries into the branches
items.bodyMarkdown:
A support queue labels a ticket by the number of hours it has waited. The policy says urgent at twenty-four hours, normal from eight hours, and low below eight. The words "at" and "from" matter: a ticket waiting exactly twenty-four hours must be urgent.

An if statement evaluates a condition and runs its branch when that condition is truthy. An else if is considered only when earlier conditions were false. This ordering is part of the program's behavior. If you check hours >= 8 first and immediately return "normal", an urgent ticket also matches that broader condition. Check the most restrictive high threshold first, or use nonoverlapping ranges.

Translate the policy into examples before writing the branches. A ticket at 7.9 hours is low, at 8 is normal, at 23.9 is normal, and at 24 is urgent. These examples describe the contract independently of any particular implementation. They also distinguish >= from >, a one-character difference that can create a real service-level defect.

A boundary can describe a count, a position, or an interval. Arrays use positions from zero through length minus one. A loop using index <= items.length takes one step beyond the last item. By contrast, a policy accepting up to five attachments is inclusive: count <= 5. There is no universally correct comparison operator; the domain decides.

Use early returns when they make the decisions easy to read. Once a branch returns, later branches do not execute. Keep invalid-input handling separate from classification when the caller needs a different error outcome. In these exercises the input is already a finite nonnegative number, so the classifier does not need to invent a policy for strings or negative values.

When repairing a boundary defect, keep the surrounding behavior stable. Write the failing exact-threshold example first, fix the comparison, then check neighboring values and a distant ordinary case. A test using only a very large value would pass both a correct inclusive implementation and an incorrect exclusive one. Meaningful boundary tests make those competing implementations disagree.
objectives: Translate inclusive numeric thresholds into ordered branches.
Test values immediately below, at, and above a boundary.
commonMistakes: Checking a broad lower threshold before a higher one.
Replacing inclusive language with an exclusive comparison.
Testing only values far from a threshold.
items.summary: Order overlapping conditions deliberately and turn every boundary into concrete neighboring examples.

items.title: Trace the first match

items.title: Control scope and side effects
items.bodyMarkdown:
Two screens use the same ticket object. A formatter unexpectedly changes its title, and the second screen now displays a value it never requested. The formatter returned useful text, but it also changed shared state. That extra effect makes the application harder to reason about.

A function receives arguments through local parameter bindings. It can create additional local bindings and return a value to its caller. A variable declared inside a function is not automatically available outside it. With let and const, a block creates another scope. An inner declaration can use the same name as an outer declaration; this is shadowing, and it does not update the outer binding.

Passing an object does not make a private copy of the object. The parameter and the caller's variable can refer to the same object. Assigning ticket.title changes that shared object. Reassigning the local parameter to a different object changes only the local binding. This distinction explains why "arguments are passed by value" does not mean object mutations are isolated.

A pure function produces its result from its inputs without changing external state. For the same inputs it returns the same result, without reading a clock or random source. Pure functions are particularly useful for validation, classification, and state transitions. You can test them directly without constructing a browser or database, and callers can reuse them without anticipating hidden writes.

Purity is a design choice for a boundary, not a requirement that every application function avoid effects. Saving a ticket necessarily changes a database. Keep that operation explicit and separate from helpers that calculate a display label or validate a count. The small helper becomes easy to test, while the surrounding operation owns persistence and error handling.

When investigating unexpected mutation, retain the original input and inspect it after the call. A test that checks only the return value can miss the defect. In this platform, function cases can also require the JSON input to remain unchanged. Use that feedback to distinguish an incorrect result from a correct result produced with an unintended side effect. Later lessons will show how copying each changed object level supports immutable updates.

Return a calculated result without changing caller-owned data.
commonMistakes: Assuming object parameters are deep copies.
Confusing a new binding with a new object.
Testing the output while ignoring unintended input changes.
items.summary: Keep calculations local and make externally visible changes explicit.

items.title: Change records without hidden mutation
items.bodyMarkdown:
A ticket has a title and an assignee record. You want to change the assignee's display name while preserving the original ticket for an undo operation. Copying the outer ticket is a useful start, but it does not automatically copy the nested assignee.

An object maps property names to values. Dot notation reads a known property, such as ticket.title. Bracket notation reads a property using an expression, such as ticket[fieldName]. If ticket.assignee is null, reading ticket.assignee.name throws because there is no object at that boundary. Optional chaining can express an optional read, and a fallback can give the interface a deliberate label.

The spread syntax creates a new outer object containing the source's enumerable own properties. For plain JSON records, {...ticket} copies the property values. A nested object value is still a reference to that same nested object. Consequently, changing copy.assignee.name can change ticket.assignee.name too. This is what a shallow copy means.

To update a nested field immutably, make a new object at every level along the changed path. The other branches can keep their references when you do not change them. That is enough to preserve the old record and gives tools such as React a new top-level identity to observe. It is usually clearer than deep-cloning an entire application state tree.

Property order in an object literal matters when names repeat. In {...ticket, title: nextTitle}, the new title wins. In {title: nextTitle, ...ticket}, the old ticket title overwrites it. Neither form changes ticket directly, but only one implements the intended update.

Begin with a precise contract: which field changes, what stays the same, and whether the input may be modified. Our update helper changes only the nested assignee name on records that always contain an assignee object. It preserves the ticket ID, title, and other assignee fields. Its cases compare the returned JSON and the original input after execution. This catches both dropping unrelated fields and returning the right answer by mutating the caller's data.
objectives: Read a nested object safely.
Copy each changed level of an object.
commonMistakes: Treating object spread as a deep clone.
Spreading the old record after the replacement field.
Dropping unrelated fields while constructing the update.

items.title: Select records, then transform them
items.bodyMarkdown:
A queue should show only open tickets and display their titles. This requirement contains two independent operations: decide which records belong, then decide what representation each selected record should have.

Array.filter calls a predicate for each existing element and returns a new array containing the elements for which the predicate is truthy. The predicate answers a yes-or-no question. Array.map calls a transformation for each existing element and returns the resulting values. On the ordinary dense arrays used here, map preserves the number of elements. Returning false from a map callback does not remove the corresponding position; it stores false there.

The order is often filter first, map second. First select tickets whose status is exactly "open". Then turn each selected ticket into its title. The resulting titles keep the order of the selected source records. An empty input produces an empty output naturally, without a special branch.

Strict comparison makes the selection policy visible. A status "Open" is different from "open" unless the contract explicitly allows case normalization. Do not silently normalize values because it makes a sample pass: your implementation should match the stated domain rule. Similarly, counting all records is not equivalent to counting open records just because the first fixture happens to contain only open tickets.

Both methods create a new outer array, but their callbacks can still mutate referenced objects. A predicate that assigns ticket.status has a side effect even when the method itself returns a new array. Keep callbacks focused on reading and returning values. A loop is also a valid implementation when it preserves the same behavior and input contract.

Test the empty collection, no matches, all matches, and a mixture with similar-looking nonmatches. For a title projection, include distinct titles so accidental repetition is visible. Check ordering where it matters. These cases describe the observable result rather than requiring a particular use of map or filter, leaving room for an equally correct loop.

When debugging a chain, inspect the intermediate value. If the first operation returns booleans, a later operation expecting ticket records cannot read title. Naming that intermediate result often makes the mismatch obvious before you change the code.
objectives: Distinguish selection with filter from transformation with map.
Count matching records without mutating input.
items.workedExampleMarkdown:
~~~js
const openTitles = tickets
  .filter(ticket => ticket.status === "open")
  .map(ticket => ticket.title);
~~~
The first result contains ticket records; the second contains title strings.

items.title: Look up and aggregate deliberately
items.bodyMarkdown:
A ticket dashboard asks two different questions: "Who owns this ticket?" and "How many tickets have each status?" The first needs a lookup; the second needs an aggregation. Choosing a clear result shape makes both operations easier to verify.

Array.find returns the first matching element, or undefined when no match exists. It is a useful choice for a small list or a one-off lookup. The return value is not guaranteed to be a record. A caller that immediately reads find(...).name assumes a successful match and can crash when fixture or API data changes. Check the missing case and choose a deliberate fallback or error.

A Map associates keys with values and is useful for repeated lookups. Its get operation also needs a missing-key policy. A plain object is often a convenient JSON result for a small, fixed set of category counts. When keys come from arbitrary external strings, do not casually treat every inherited object property as a normal bucket; use Map or an explicitly safe dictionary approach. In this lesson the statuses are a fixed set.

Aggregation combines multiple records into a smaller summary. A counting loop starts with an initial result and updates one category per record. The initial state defines the empty-input answer. For our queue, open, pending, and closed all appear in the returned result, even when their counts are zero. This stable shape simplifies display code because it does not have to invent defaults.

You can express the same calculation with reduce, but a compact expression is not inherently clearer. What matters is that the accumulator begins correctly, each input contributes once, and the function does not alter caller-owned records. A local accumulator created inside the function can be updated safely; it is not shared external state.

Test repeated categories, absent categories, and the empty list. A fixture with one record in each category cannot distinguish a real count from a mistaken presence flag. Include at least two records with the same status. For lookup code, cover both present and missing IDs. These tests force the implementation to address the questions the screen actually asks, including the cases that a happy-path demo does not reveal.
objectives: Choose a lookup or aggregation that matches the question.
Handle missing records explicitly.
commonMistakes: Assuming find always succeeds.
Counting category presence rather than repeated records.

items.title: Follow promises through a call chain
items.bodyMarkdown:
The ticket page starts loading records and immediately tries to display their length. Sometimes the developer sees a promise instead of an array. The problem is a boundary between starting work and receiving its eventual result.

A promise represents an operation that may still be pending and will eventually fulfill with a value or reject with a reason. Calling an asynchronous API usually returns that promise before the work finishes. The rest of the current synchronous code can continue. An async function also returns a promise, even if its body returns a plain value.

Inside an async function, await pauses that function's continuation until the promise settles. It does not freeze the entire browser. A fulfilled promise supplies a value; a rejected promise makes the await expression throw. This allows ordinary try/catch syntax to handle an asynchronous failure at the place that awaits it.

The order of statements still matters. In the prepared example, "start" and "end" are logged by synchronous code. A then callback on an already fulfilled promise is scheduled after that synchronous work, so "loaded" appears later. This small example demonstrates scheduling without depending on network timing. A real request can take an unpredictable amount of time.

A missing await can change both values and error handling. If loadTickets returns a promise, loadTickets().length is not the length of its future array. Similarly, a try block that merely starts a promise without awaiting or returning it does not automatically catch a later rejection. Connect the promise to a caller that owns the outcome.

Avoid adding await mechanically to every operation. Synchronous calculations do not need it, and awaiting independent requests one at a time can serialize work unnecessarily. Begin by drawing dependencies: which result does the next step need? Keep dependent work in order and handle failures at a level that can explain them to the user.

For these browser lessons, asynchronous network examples are reading exercises with prepared traces. The isolated function runner intentionally does not expose fetch or timers. Local project missions provide the realistic request environment, where you can test delayed responses and verify that loading and error states follow the actual operation.

items.title: Read an HTTP result as a contract
items.bodyMarkdown:
A ticket create request reaches the server and returns a validation error. The network connection worked, but the requested business operation did not. A client that treats every received response as success will show the wrong message and may erase the user's draft.

An HTTP method communicates the requested operation. In our ticket contract, GET reads tickets and POST creates one. PATCH updates selected fields of an existing ticket. A route path identifies the resource or collection. The JSON body contains the supplied data. These are separate parts of a request, and the server validates each boundary.

A response status gives a broad outcome. Successful creation commonly uses 201. A missing or inaccessible resource can use 404 under a documented policy. This course's API uses 422 for well-formed but invalid field values and 409 for a conflict with current stored state. Status conventions need an explicit contract; do not assume every service uses the same validation status.

The browser fetch promise normally fulfills when an HTTP response is available, including a 404 or 500 response. It rejects for certain request or network failures. Therefore a catch block alone is not enough to classify HTTP errors. Inspect response.ok or response.status before treating the body as a successful resource.

Reading a JSON body is another asynchronous operation and can fail if the response is not valid JSON. A proxy might return an HTML error page, or a server contract might allow an empty body. Parse according to the endpoint contract, handle parsing failure, and avoid reading the same response body twice. Do not expose raw HTML or a server stack trace as a user-facing explanation.

An error message should tell the user what action is useful. A field validation response can attach an error to the title input and preserve the entered text. An unavailable ticket can show a clear missing-resource state. A server failure can offer a retry when the operation's retry semantics permit it.

Use prepared response fixtures to exercise these decisions. A successful JSON example proves only one path. Include a validation response, a missing record, and a malformed body so the interface demonstrates that it understands both the HTTP envelope and the application data inside it.

items.title: Handle failure and stale responses
items.bodyMarkdown:
The owner searches for "printer" and then quickly replaces it with "network". The network search finishes first. A slower printer response arrives later and overwrites the screen. Every request succeeded, yet the interface now displays results for a query the owner no longer wants.

A race occurs when the visible outcome depends on the timing of independent operations. Sending requests in order does not guarantee receiving responses in that order. The application needs a rule for deciding which result still belongs to the current view. For a search box, that is usually the most recent query.

Cancellation can stop unnecessary work. AbortController supplies a signal to compatible APIs such as fetch, and abort requests cancellation. Handle cancellation as an expected state rather than an alarming server failure. Cancellation is not a guarantee that the server undid a committed write, and a response may already have reached another stage of your code.

A current-request identifier or query-key check gives the view an additional acceptance boundary. Capture the request's identity when starting it, and apply its result only if it still matches the active request. This prevents stale success or failure callbacks from replacing newer state. A query library can manage much of this relationship when keys accurately include the search parameters.

Retries need a different decision. A temporary failure on a read may justify a bounded retry with a delay. A validation failure will not improve until the input changes. A create request that times out may already have committed, so blindly repeating it can create duplicates. Later lessons introduce idempotency keys to make specific write retries safe.

Keep the user's input visible during failures. A retry should repeat the intended operation with a clear state, and the UI should prevent accidental duplicate submissions while work is pending. A cancellation button should leave the screen in a usable state and should not silently mark unfinished work as saved.

A good test controls response timing instead of hoping a race occurs. Start request A, then B; resolve B first and A second. Assert that B remains visible. Add a cancelled-request case and a retryable failure fixture. These tests describe the timing contract directly and can reproduce a defect that appears only intermittently in manual testing.

items.title: Use types to expose missing values
items.bodyMarkdown:
A ticket formatter expects a string title, but a caller passes a number. JavaScript may run until the formatter calls a string method and fails. TypeScript can identify this mismatch before the program executes, provided the value flows through a checked type boundary.

Type annotations describe the values code expects. A parameter annotated string accepts text, while a return annotation documents and checks the function's result. Inference often supplies local types automatically, so you do not need to repeat every obvious annotation. An explicit function boundary is useful when a changing implementation could accidentally alter a public contract.

With strict null checking, a value declared Ticket | null cannot be treated as a Ticket until code handles the null possibility. A condition can narrow the value in one branch. If the value is null, return a deliberate fallback; otherwise read the record. This is the same runtime decision the application needs, now checked by the compiler.

An optional property may be undefined. Optional chaining stops a property read at a nullish boundary, and the nullish coalescing operator supplies a fallback only for null or undefined. Unlike the logical OR operator, it preserves valid falsy values such as an empty string or numeric zero. Choose the fallback according to the domain rather than using it to conceal malformed data.

The non-null assertion operator tells the compiler to trust you, but it does not insert a runtime check. A cast also does not convert a value or fetch missing data. These tools can be appropriate where an invariant is independently established, but they are poor repairs for a real optional-access defect.

Compiler success is one kind of evidence. It cannot establish that external JSON follows your declaration, nor can it prove a numeric calculation implements the business policy. Run runtime validation at external boundaries and behavioral tests on the checked implementation. In these exercises, TypeScript source must pass semantic compilation before the isolated JavaScript behavior is evaluated. A type annotation that disagrees with the body is therefore a failed submission even if a transpiler could erase it.

items.title: Model alternatives with discriminated unions
items.bodyMarkdown:
An API panel can be loading, failed, or successful. A loose object with optional data and optional error allows combinations that do not make sense: success without data, or a loading state carrying an old error. A discriminated union describes each valid alternative separately.

The alternatives share a property with different literal values, such as kind: "loading", kind: "error", and kind: "success". Each alternative contains only the fields it needs. The success member includes data; the error member includes message. Checking kind lets TypeScript narrow the value to the matching member, so fields become available where they are valid.

This model supports clear rendering. The loading branch shows progress, the error branch offers a useful message and retry, and the success branch renders data. Empty successful data is still a success state, often with its own empty-list presentation. Do not confuse an empty collection with a request that has not completed.

A switch statement makes a closed set of alternatives easy to review. To detect forgotten cases after adding a new alternative, assign the remaining value to never in a final exhaustive branch. If all alternatives have been handled, no value remains. If a new member is unhandled, the compiler reports that it cannot be assigned to never.

A type assertion can silence the error while leaving the underlying state problem untouched. Casting an arbitrary string to TicketStatus does not validate it. At an external boundary, inspect the value and construct a valid union member only after validation. Inside checked application code, rely on narrowing rather than repeatedly asserting the desired shape.

The browser exercise maps each allowed ticket status to a display label. It is intentionally a small pure function so you can focus on alternatives and exhaustive behavior. The tests include every current member, and semantic compilation checks the annotations. When you extend the status type later, update the cases and the content mastery revision because the learning contract has changed.

Use discriminated unions where the alternatives affect behavior. A simple string field does not need an elaborate state model merely for style. The benefit comes from preventing impossible combinations and making each required branch explicit to both a reader and the compiler.

items.title: Describe shapes and preserve useful types
items.bodyMarkdown:
Several screens need a list of record IDs. Tickets have a title and status; people have a name and team. The helper needs only an id, so requiring the whole Ticket type would couple a simple operation to an unrelated domain shape.

TypeScript primarily compares object types structurally. A value with the required properties and compatible property types can satisfy a contract even when it was declared using another interface name. Naming an interface does not make its values a separate runtime class. Additional properties can remain on an existing value, although fresh object literals also receive excess-property checks in common assignment contexts.

A generic type parameter expresses a relationship between types across a function. The constraint T extends {id:string} says each accepted record must have a string id, while T can retain additional information supplied by the caller. The helper can safely read id because the constraint guarantees that part of the shape.

Use a generic when the relationship matters. A helper that merely accepts a string and returns its length does not become better by adding an unused type parameter. Conversely, a function that returns an input record can preserve that record's richer type through T instead of widening it to a minimal shape and losing useful fields.

A declared interface does not inspect JSON. When data arrives from a server, a type assertion or generic fetch helper can create a false sense of certainty. Runtime parsing must validate the required fields before application code treats the value as a trusted record. The static type then describes the result of that validation.

The practice helper returns IDs from records in their original order without modifying the array. Empty input returns an empty array. Duplicate IDs remain duplicated because this helper performs projection, not uniqueness enforcement. Naming that distinction prevents an implementation from adding a policy the caller did not request.

Read compiler errors by identifying the relationship that failed. A numeric id cannot satisfy a string-id constraint. That error might mean the caller needs a different contract or an explicit conversion at a validated boundary. Changing everything to any removes the signal instead of resolving the mismatch. Keep the narrowest useful contract and let the caller retain its own domain information.
objectives: Compare structural object contracts.
Constrain reusable helpers while retaining their input relationship.
commonMistakes: Assuming interface names create runtime validation.
Using any to erase a meaningful constraint failure.
Adding a generic parameter that expresses no relationship.
items.summary: Use structural requirements for what you read and generics for relationships you preserve.

items.title: Web interface fundamentals
items.bodyMarkdown: Build semantic controls, adaptable layouts, and understandable states.

items.title: Start with meaningful controls
items.bodyMarkdown:
A create-ticket form can look complete while remaining difficult to use without a mouse. A nearby word may look like a label, but the browser needs a real association to expose the control's purpose and make label clicks focus it.

Use a label element with a for attribute matching the input's unique id, or place the input inside its label. In React, the property is htmlFor. Keep a visible label when possible so the field remains understandable after the user types. Placeholder text is a hint inside an empty control; it disappears and should not carry the entire labeling responsibility.

Choose elements according to the interaction. An anchor with an href navigates to a resource. A button performs an action. Native buttons already participate in keyboard navigation and have expected activation behavior. A clickable div requires you to rebuild these semantics, and adding only an onClick handler leaves important interactions missing.

A form groups controls and supplies a submission event. Handle submission at the form boundary so clicking the submit button and submitting from the keyboard follow the same validation path. In a client-rendered application, prevent the default navigation when the JavaScript handler intentionally owns submission. Keep the server's validation as the authoritative protection for stored data.

Button type matters inside a form. A save button can explicitly be type="submit". A separate action such as showing a preview should use type="button" so it does not accidentally trigger form submission. Clear types make the behavior visible in code review and avoid surprises when a component is reused inside a form.

Native required and input-type constraints provide useful browser feedback, but they do not replace the full business contract. A required text field can still contain whitespace, so a trimmed-title rule needs a corresponding application check. Associate the resulting message with the field and retain the entered value.

Verify the form using only the keyboard. Move through controls in the expected order, activate actions, and submit both valid and invalid data. Then inspect accessible names through browser tools or role-based tests. These checks reveal whether the interface communicates its behavior, rather than merely painting a familiar-looking set of boxes.
objectives: Associate labels with form controls.
Use native interaction semantics for links, buttons, and submission.

~~~html
<form>
  <label for="ticket-title">Title</label>
  <input id="ticket-title" name="title" required>
  <button type="submit">Create ticket</button>
  <button type="button">Preview</button>
</form>
~~~
The label identifies the field, and each button declares its intended form behavior.

Replacing a native button with an unfocusable clickable div.
Letting a secondary form action submit accidentally.

items.title: Let layout adapt to available space
items.bodyMarkdown:
A ticket detail page works on a laptop but forces sideways scrolling on a phone. The cause may be a fixed-width panel, an inflexible grid track, or one long line of code. Shrinking every font is unlikely to address the actual layout constraint.

Start with the containing block and the width a component is allowed to use. A fixed width of 960 pixels cannot fit inside a 360-pixel viewport. A maximum width combined with a fluid available width can keep a readable desktop measure while allowing the panel to shrink. Include padding in your reasoning; border-box sizing makes the declared width include padding and borders.

CSS Grid describes rows and columns, while Flexbox is useful for distributing items along one primary direction. Two equal grid columns can use repeat(2, minmax(0, 1fr)). The zero minimum allows tracks to shrink below their content's automatic minimum. Without an appropriate minimum, long content can force an apparently flexible column wider than the available space.

A media query can change a two-column detail layout to one column when the content no longer fits comfortably. Choose the breakpoint from the layout's needs rather than assuming every device belongs to one exact category. Preserve the reading order in the document so the stacked layout remains understandable and keyboard navigation follows the content naturally.

Long unbroken text and preformatted code need a local overflow policy. A code block can scroll horizontally inside its panel while the page itself remains within the viewport. Ordinary text may wrap with an appropriate overflow-wrap rule. Hiding page overflow can conceal buttons or data and does not prove the layout is usable.

Inspect the actual overflowing element in browser tools. Compare its computed width with its parent and temporarily remove suspicious width or minimum-width rules. This creates evidence for a focused fix. Check both a short title and an unusually long title, because sample content can hide the constraint.

The local mini-task starts with a deliberately oversized panel. Repair its CSS, then test at 360 pixels and a wide viewport. Confirm that all controls remain reachable and that any code scrolling belongs to the code block. Record your observations against the rubric; this task is self-assessed, while later missions add browser checks to the full feature.
objectives: Predict simple grid behavior.
Repair narrow-screen overflow without hiding essential content.
commonMistakes: Masking page overflow with overflow-x:hidden.
Ignoring automatic minimum sizes of grid children.
Testing only short sample text on a wide screen.

items.title: Communicate state beyond color
items.bodyMarkdown:
A title field turns red after submission, but nothing explains what went wrong. A person who cannot distinguish the color, uses a screen reader, or simply does not know the rule has no clear repair path. State needs a meaningful message and a relationship to the affected control.

Write a concise field error such as "Enter a title with at least one non-space character." Keep it visible and associate it with the input using aria-describedby. Set aria-invalid when the value has failed validation. The label still identifies the field; the error description adds context rather than replacing the label.

Accessible names tell users what a control does. Visible button text often supplies the best name directly. An icon-only action needs an appropriate name such as "Close ticket details". Avoid an aria-label that contradicts the visible wording, because speech users may try to activate what they can see. Decorative icons should not add distracting duplicate text.

Dynamic updates also affect orientation. After a failed submission, move focus only when doing so helps the user reach the error, such as focusing the first invalid field or a useful error summary. Do not move focus on every keystroke or every successful background refresh. Unexpected focus changes interrupt reading and input.

A dialog needs a clear name, an appropriate initial focus target, keyboard containment while open, and restoration to a useful trigger when it closes. Adding role="dialog" alone does not implement those behaviors. Prefer an established accessible primitive or carefully verify the complete interaction. The same principle applies to menus and custom controls.

Status announcements should be proportionate. A saving indicator can use a polite status region without repeatedly interrupting the user. Urgent validation feedback may need stronger attention, but announcing every character typed creates noise. Test the actual sequence rather than merely counting ARIA attributes.

The review exercise asks you to walk through keyboard focus before, during, and after an interaction. Observe the visible focus indicator, control names, error relationships, and return destination. Automated tests can catch missing labels and some structural defects, while a deliberate keyboard and assistive-technology review checks whether the experience remains understandable over time.

items.title: React fundamentals
items.bodyMarkdown: Trace props, state transitions, and synchronization boundaries.

items.title: Give components clear inputs
items.bodyMarkdown:
A ticket row needs a title, status, and link to its detail page. It does not need to know how the database connection is configured. A component becomes easier to understand when its inputs describe what it renders and its callbacks describe the actions it can request.

A function component receives props and returns a description of the interface using JSX. Expressions inside braces read JavaScript values. Passing title="Printer" gives the component a string prop; passing count={3} gives it a number. The rendered output follows those values for that render.

Treat props as read-only. A child that changes ticket.title through its prop object can affect shared data without the parent owning the change. Instead, the child calls a supplied callback such as onRename(nextTitle), and the owning component or data layer decides how to update state and persistence. This makes the direction of information easier to trace.

A useful boundary often follows a coherent interaction or presentation responsibility. A TicketRow can display one record, a TicketList can render a collection, and a page can coordinate route parameters and server data. Avoid splitting every line into a component merely to reduce file length. A reader should be able to explain the purpose of each boundary.

When rendering a list, React uses keys to relate sibling elements across renders. A stable record ID usually expresses that identity. An array index can associate the wrong local state with a row when insertion, deletion, or reordering changes positions. A random key changes every render and can cause unnecessary remounting. Keys are local to the sibling collection, and they are not automatically passed as an ordinary prop.

items.title: Calculate the next state from the right snapshot
items.bodyMarkdown:
A button is intended to add two to a counter. Its handler calls setCount(count + 1) twice, but the count rises only once. Both calls used the same count value captured by that render, so both requested the same replacement.

State belongs to a particular render snapshot. Calling a setter schedules a later render; it does not rewrite the local count variable in the already running handler. This makes a handler's values predictable while it runs, but it means several updates based on previous state need the right form.

A functional update supplies a calculation such as previous => previous + 1. React can apply queued updater functions in order, passing each the result of the earlier update. Two such increments therefore compose. Keep updater functions pure because the framework may evaluate them in development checks, and side effects should not be hidden inside a calculation of state.

Objects and arrays in state also need deliberate updates. Mutating an existing array and passing back that same reference can obscure the change and corrupt earlier snapshots. Create a new array and replace only the records that change. A pure helper can express the transition independently of React and is easy to test in the browser runner.

Our practice transition closes a ticket with a matching ID. It returns a collection in the original order, preserves unrelated fields, and leaves the input untouched. If the ID is missing, the returned JSON represents the same records; the helper must not silently close a different ticket. The contract does not require a particular implementation or reference reuse strategy.

Separate state transitions from persistence. Updating a local ticket to closed can make the interface responsive, but it does not establish that the server accepted the change. An optimistic UI needs a defined error and reconciliation policy. The next chapter introduces server state and form submission as distinct concerns.

To debug state behavior, record the render values, the queued action, and the expected next state. Test two queued increments for snapshot mistakes, and retain the original array when testing an immutable update. These examples target the state model directly instead of merely verifying that a button's event handler was called.

Implement immutable state transitions.

items.title: Derive values before adding an effect
items.bodyMarkdown:
A ticket list stores both allTickets and openTickets in state. An effect updates openTickets whenever allTickets changes. The application now has two representations of the same information, and a missing dependency can leave the second one stale.

If a value can be calculated from current props and state during render, derive it there. Filtering tickets by the current status selection is a calculation, not synchronization with an external system. Keeping it as a second state variable introduces an additional update and an invariant that the code must maintain.

Effects are useful when a component needs to synchronize with something outside React's rendering calculation. Examples include subscribing to an event source, connecting to a browser API, or coordinating an external widget. The effect describes setup, and its cleanup reverses or stops the relevant work when dependencies change or the component is removed.

Dependencies describe the reactive values an effect reads. An effect that fetches by ticketId but uses an empty dependency array can keep showing the first ticket after navigation. Suppressing the dependency warning does not repair that relationship. Include the changing value, or restructure the code so the effect has the correct boundary. For server data, a query abstraction often expresses resource identity and cancellation more clearly.

Cleanup must correspond to the work started. An event listener should be removed using the same listener identity. A request can be aborted or its obsolete result ignored. Development checks that run setup and cleanup more than once can reveal code that assumed setup happened only once forever. Treat these checks as evidence about missing cleanup, not a reason to disable them.

Memoization is a performance tool, not a substitute for a correct data model. A small filter is often fine directly in render. Measure expensive calculations before adding caching, and ensure any dependency list remains complete. The correct result should not depend on a cache being retained.

Review an effect by asking what external system it synchronizes, which values determine that synchronization, and how it stops old work. If there is no external system and the body merely copies a calculation into state, the simpler repair may be to remove the effect and derive the value where it is used.
objectives: Distinguish render calculations from external synchronization.
Review effect dependencies and cleanup.
commonMistakes: Using effects to maintain redundant derived state.
Omitting a reactive dependency to avoid reruns.
Adding a listener without corresponding cleanup.

items.title: React forms and API data
items.bodyMarkdown: Coordinate drafts, server snapshots, and accessible feature journeys.

items.title: Keep form input and submission in sync
items.bodyMarkdown:
A create form receives a value prop from state, but typing does not change what appears. The browser produces an input event; the component must update the state that supplies the next value. Without that update, React renders the same controlled value again.

A controlled text input receives a string value and an onChange handler that stores the current input text. Initialize the state consistently, usually with an empty string. A checkbox is controlled through checked rather than the text value property. Keep the displayed input responsive; a slow save operation should not delay the local typing update.

Separate the draft from the normalized submission value. Trimming the entire field on every keystroke can move the caret or prevent the user from entering intended spaces while editing. Instead, preserve the editing string and normalize at the validation or submission boundary. Show a useful error when the trimmed value is blank or exceeds the documented bound.

Submission has a lifecycle. Validate first; if invalid, keep the draft and explain the problem. If valid, mark the operation pending, prevent duplicate submission, and await the API result. Only confirmed success should trigger the success behavior, such as clearing the form or navigating to the new ticket. A failure should preserve the user’s work and offer a correction or retry.

A disabled button provides immediate feedback, but the handler should also guard against a second in-flight operation. The server still owns durable duplicate protection where retries can repeat a write. These layers solve related problems at different boundaries; one does not erase the need for the other.

Use a pure validation helper to make the input policy easy to test. Our helper returns a normalized title and either null or one error code. It checks the trimmed length, so leading and trailing spaces do not change the accepted content. Test blank, whitespace-only, exact-bound, and over-bound values.

Then test the form integration with a deliberately delayed API response. While pending, another activation should not start another request. If the request fails, the text should remain. A successful response should produce the documented next state. These observations establish that input, validation, and submission work together rather than merely proving a setter exists.

Validate and submit while preserving recoverable draft state.

Clearing text before an awaited save succeeds.
Using disabled appearance as the only duplicate guard.

items.title: Treat server data as a changing snapshot
items.bodyMarkdown:
A ticket list displays "No tickets" before its first request finishes. A moment later rows appear. The empty message was misleading because the application had no successful data yet; it confused absence of a response with a successful response containing no records.

Server state has an external owner. The browser holds a snapshot that can become stale while another device changes the database. A query abstraction can manage fetching, caching, retries, and refetching, but the view still needs an explicit interpretation of its states. Loading is not the same as empty success, and an error is not an empty collection.

A query key identifies which resource snapshot the cache represents. Include parameters that change the result, such as status filter and page cursor. If all filtered lists share one key, data for one filter can appear under another. Stable keys connect the data lifecycle to the visible question the user asked.

Background refetching differs from the initial load. When useful cached data exists, the view may keep it visible while indicating refresh activity. If that refresh fails, preserve the known data with an appropriate stale or error message instead of blanking the interface without explanation. The exact policy belongs to the product, but it should be deliberate.

An API adapter translates transport details into an application contract. A pure mapper can turn a validated response into the labels and stable IDs a component needs. It should preserve ordering and handle documented nullable fields. Runtime validation belongs before trusting an external shape; a mapper typed against validated input should not pretend to inspect arbitrary malformed JSON.

After a successful mutation, update or invalidate the relevant query data so the list reflects the change. Avoid maintaining a disconnected manual copy that drifts from the query cache. On refocus or reconnect, refresh according to the freshness policy so work from another device can become visible.

Test the view with separate fixtures for pending, empty success, populated success, initial error, and failed background refresh. A delayed response exposes premature empty messages. Changing the filter exposes cache-key mistakes. These cases check whether the screen tells the truth about the snapshot it actually has.

items.title: Compose an accessible feature journey
items.bodyMarkdown:
A ticket detail feature combines routing, server data, controls, and feedback. Each part can work in isolation while their integration still fails: the route might supply the wrong ID, an error might replace the wrong record, or focus might disappear after a save.

Begin with the user’s journey. Opening a detail link establishes a resource ID and starts loading. A successful response shows that ticket; a missing-resource result shows the documented unavailable state. Editing creates local draft state. Saving enters pending, then either confirms success or preserves the draft with a useful error. These states should correspond to actual events rather than optimistic assumptions.

Give each layer a clear responsibility. The route identifies the resource. The adapter enforces the HTTP response contract and validates data. The query layer owns the server snapshot. The form owns transient editing input. Presentational components expose labels, errors, and controls. These boundaries allow focused tests without turning the page into disconnected pieces that cannot coordinate.

Accessibility applies across the transitions. A loading indicator should have meaningful text. An error must be discoverable and associated with the relevant action or field. A detail heading identifies the current resource. Keyboard users should reach edit, save, cancel, and navigation controls in a sensible order. Pending work should not silently steal focus.

A component integration test renders enough of the feature to exercise the relationship between these parts. Use a memory router with a known ticket path and a controlled adapter fixture. Avoid inspecting private state variable names, because a sound internal refactor should not invalidate a behavior contract.

Control timing for a delayed save, then assert that duplicate activation produces only one request. Reject a validation response and check that the title remains editable with its error. Navigate to another ticket while the first request is pending and ensure old results do not replace the new detail. These are meaningful integration boundaries.

A small end-to-end browser journey complements those tests by exercising the real rendered page and network path. It can verify keyboard reachability and narrow-screen fit. It does not replace database tests or prove every accessibility requirement. Combine the evidence according to what each layer can actually observe.

items.title: Make the route a clear boundary
items.bodyMarkdown:
A request reaches GET /tickets/17. The route parameter is text from an external client, not a trusted database ID merely because the URL looks familiar. The handler must turn the request into an authorized, validated operation before it reads or changes application data.

A route combines an HTTP method and path pattern with a handler. Path parameters identify resources, query parameters refine an operation, and a body supplies data for relevant methods. Keep these sources distinct in the contract. A list page size belongs in a bounded query parameter; a new ticket title belongs in the creation body.

The boundary typically authenticates the caller, validates the request shape, applies resource access policy, performs the operation, and maps the result to the response contract. The exact framework hook order should be explicit, especially where parsing and authentication interact. Business code should receive validated values and a trusted identity rather than rereading arbitrary request fields.

Parsing is not always validation. parseInt("17junk", 10) returns 17 because it accepts a numeric prefix. If the route contract allows only canonical positive decimal IDs, that input must be rejected rather than partially accepted. Check the complete string and the permitted numeric range before returning a usable value.

A pure parser makes these rules easy to test. It can return a number or null without knowing about HTTP replies or database connections. The route then maps null to the documented invalid-parameter response. Separating this calculation does not require a large architecture; one small helper can provide a useful boundary.

Keep business operations focused as well. A createTicket service can enforce a meaningful invariant and persistence operation without choosing CSS messages. The route translates transport input and output around that operation. This separation allows the same rule to be tested without constructing an entire browser.

When reviewing a handler, follow the data: where did this value come from, when was it checked, which owner does this operation use, and what can the client observe? A passing happy-path response does not establish that invalid parameters are rejected before data access. Add malformed, zero, negative, and out-of-range cases so the boundary itself is verified.

Parse route parameters according to an explicit contract.

items.title: Validate actual request data
items.bodyMarkdown:
The handler is written in TypeScript and declares a body type with title: string. A caller still sends title as an array. The compiler checked the program text, but it did not control the bytes arriving over HTTP. Runtime validation must establish which values the operation can trust.

Start from unknown external data. A JSON parser establishes that the bytes form JSON; it does not establish the business shape. The body may be null, an array, or an object with missing and unexpected properties. A runtime schema or explicit parser checks the permitted shape and returns a validated value or a structured error.

Validation has several dimensions. Type checks distinguish strings from numbers and arrays. Presence checks identify missing required data. Bounds limit size and resource use. Domain checks constrain values such as status. Normalization, such as trimming a title, should have a documented relationship to those checks so the client and server agree on what will be stored.

Avoid accepting everything by coercion. String({}) produces a string, but it is not a meaningful ticket title. If the contract requires a string, reject an object rather than turning its default representation into stored text. Where conversion is allowed, name it explicitly and test its edge cases.

Validation should finish before a write begins. Invalid input must not create a partial ticket or comment. Database constraints remain valuable as an independent guard for relationships and uniqueness, but they do not replace useful field errors or all request-size limits. Each boundary protects the invariants it can enforce.

A schema library reduces repetitive parsing and can provide precise field paths. Treat the schema as trusted application code, not arbitrary instructions uploaded by a client. Limit request body size before expensive processing, and avoid performing unbounded external work inside a basic shape check.

Our pure helper validates a title value and returns either a normalized string result or a small error code. This is intentionally narrower than a full request schema. Its cases include the wrong type, whitespace, and both sides of the length bound. The route integration tests later verify that invalid complete requests return the documented error without changing database rows.

items.title: Return deliberate error contracts
items.bodyMarkdown:
A database operation throws an exception containing a query, table names, and internal paths. Returning that object directly makes debugging seem easy, but it also exposes implementation details and creates a response shape the client cannot rely on.

An API error contract separates a stable machine-readable code from a useful human message. The HTTP status gives a broad outcome, while the code identifies the application condition. A client can associate VALIDATION_FAILED with fields or REVISION_CONFLICT with a conflict screen without parsing English text.

Known domain failures deserve deliberate mappings. A missing resource can use 404, invalid field data can use 422 under this contract, and an optimistic concurrency conflict can use 409. An unexpected failure should become a generic 500 response with a safe message. Do not classify every exception as bad input, because that hides server defects and misleads clients about recovery.

Internal diagnostics belong in protected operational logs with a request identifier and appropriate redaction. The response can include that request identifier so an operator can correlate a user report with the relevant log event. Never log passwords, session tokens, or entire sensitive bodies merely because an operation failed.

Keep the mapping deterministic and small. A pure function can translate a known error code into status, code, and message. Unknown inputs map to the generic internal result. This helper should not copy arbitrary exception properties into its output. An allowlist of response fields is easier to reason about than a list of secrets that might be incomplete.

A route should preserve error semantics across its success and failure paths. Returning status 200 with an error-shaped body can make clients treat the request as successful unless that unusual contract is explicitly designed. Prefer clear documented status behavior and test it with actual requests.

Regression cases should cover every known mapping, an unknown error, and a secret-bearing internal exception at the integration boundary. Assert the safe public response and the useful request correlation, not the precise stack trace text. The goal is to make failures understandable to the client while keeping enough protected evidence for the developer to investigate the cause.

items.title: Relational persistence
items.bodyMarkdown: Model constraints, deterministic queries, and atomic changes.

items.title: Model relationships with enforceable keys
items.bodyMarkdown:
A ticket can have many comments, and every comment must belong to a real ticket. Storing all comment text in one comma-separated ticket field makes independent updates, ordering, and relationships difficult. A relational model gives each comment its own row and an explicit link to its ticket.

A table describes records with named columns and declared types. A primary key identifies each row uniquely and cannot be null. It should be stable even if a human-readable title changes. A ticket title is therefore a poor identity: two tickets can share a title, and editing text should not create a different logical ticket.

A foreign key connects a column to a referenced key in another table. Comment.ticketId can reference Ticket.id, allowing many comments to point to one ticket. The database rejects an invalid reference under that constraint. Application validation can provide a useful missing-ticket response, while the foreign key remains an independent protection against inconsistent writes.

A unique constraint expresses a different rule: a value or combination must not be duplicated within its defined scope. For example, a training import might require a unique pair of ownerId and externalTicketId. That allows different owners to reuse an external ID while preventing duplicates for one owner. A preliminary application lookup alone is vulnerable to two concurrent requests both observing absence.

Choose nullability deliberately. If every comment requires a ticket, ticketId should be non-null as well as a foreign key. Otherwise null can represent an unlinked row under normal constraint semantics. Optional fields should correspond to a real domain state, not merely a way to make insertion errors disappear.

Deletion policy also needs a decision. Should deleting a ticket remove its comments, be prevented while comments exist, or use archival instead? A foreign-key action can enforce a chosen behavior, but it should follow the product rule. Do not select cascading deletion simply because it makes a failing test pass.

Sketch the relationships before writing handlers, then verify them against concrete records. Can two comments belong to one ticket? Can a comment exist without one? Can two owners share the same external reference? These questions turn a diagram into enforceable rules and make it clear which invariants belong in the database as well as the API.

Model ticket comments as related records.
commonMistakes: Using editable display text as a stable identity.
Treating a foreign key as a guarantee that an optional column is non-null.
Enforcing uniqueness only through a check-before-insert query.

items.title: Make query order and page boundaries explicit
items.bodyMarkdown:
A ticket list shows a record twice when the owner moves to the next page. The query sorts only by createdAt, and several records share the same timestamp. The database is free to order tied rows differently, so the apparent page boundary is not a stable identity.

A SELECT query describes which columns and rows to return. WHERE filters rows; ORDER BY specifies their order; LIMIT bounds the returned count. Without an ordering contract, a list should not rely on the physical insertion or storage order. An execution plan can change while the logical data remains the same.

A deterministic order needs a tie-breaker. Ordering by createdAt and then a unique id gives every row a defined position under the chosen direction. The pagination cursor must carry enough information to continue that same order. A cursor based on createdAt alone can skip or repeat records that share the timestamp.

Offset pagination skips a specified number of rows before taking a page. It can be useful for a fixed, small dataset, but concurrent insertions or deletions can shift positions. Cursor pagination continues after a known ordered tuple. It still needs documented behavior when data changes; it is not a magic snapshot of a constantly changing database.

Bound page size at the server boundary so a client cannot request every record by passing a huge limit. Fetch one extra row if you need to determine whether another page exists, then return the requested number and a cursor based on the final returned row. The next request should use the same filter and ordering contract.

An empty page is a valid result. A missing detail resource is a different API question and usually follows a missing-record policy. Keep those outcomes distinct in both queries and UI feedback. Parameterize input values rather than constructing SQL text from untrusted strings.

Test a dataset with tied timestamps, more rows than one page, and no matches. Assert the IDs returned across consecutive pages, not merely the length of each page. Duplicate and missing IDs reveal ordering defects that a count-only assertion can miss. In the local mission, inspect the generated SQL so you can see how ORM options implement the intended database operation.
objectives: Predict filtered and ordered query results.
Review deterministic pagination with ties and empty results.
items.workedExampleMarkdown:
~~~sql
SELECT id, title
FROM ticket
WHERE status = $1
ORDER BY created_at ASC, id ASC
LIMIT $2;
~~~
The unique ID resolves timestamp ties, while parameter values stay separate from SQL syntax.

Using a nonunique timestamp as the entire page position.

items.title: Change schemas and data as deliberate operations
items.bodyMarkdown:
A deployment adds a required ticket priority column to a database that already contains thousands of rows. The application change is small, but the existing data and the older application version still matter. A migration is an operational change to a live contract, not just a generated file to run blindly.

Versioned migrations describe how a schema changes over time. Keep applied migration history immutable and add a new migration for the next change. Test the sequence on an empty database and on a representative prior schema with data. A migration that works only on a fresh database can fail when existing rows violate a new constraint.

For a required field, a staged approach may add it compatibly, backfill existing rows using an explicit rule, update application behavior, and enforce the final constraint after the data and deployed versions are ready. The exact sequence depends on the rollout, but it must account for both old and new readers and writers. Inspect generated SQL before applying it.

Transactions address a related but different boundary: a group of data changes that should commit together or not at all. Creating a ticket and its required initial event may form one atomic operation. If the event insertion fails, leaving only the ticket would violate that operation's invariant.

Within a transaction, a failure can trigger rollback so none of the grouped writes become the committed result. Keep the transaction focused and avoid waiting on slow remote services while holding database locks. External effects such as sending email do not automatically roll back with a database transaction; later chapters introduce durable job records for that coordination.

A transaction alone does not solve every concurrent race. Isolation level, locks, unique constraints, and revision checks determine how competing operations interact. Start by naming the invariant, then choose the mechanisms needed to enforce it. Do not assume wrapping a check and write in any transaction always prevents duplicates.

Verification should inject a failure between the grouped writes and inspect the final database state. For schema changes, rehearse migration and recovery on disposable data. A backup becomes useful evidence only after restoration has been tested. Document which application version remains compatible and how to recover without silently discarding legitimate writes made after deployment.
objectives: Plan a compatible migration workflow.
Identify atomic write boundaries and rollback expectations.
items.workedExampleMarkdown:
~~~text
BEGIN
  insert ticket
  insert required ticket-created event
COMMIT
If the second insert fails: ROLLBACK both writes.
~~~
The transaction boundary follows the invariant that a created ticket has its required event.
