items.title: Authentication and permissions
items.bodyMarkdown: Enforce identity, resource ownership, and safe request boundaries.

items.title: Separate identity from permission
items.bodyMarkdown:
A signed-in support agent guesses the ID of another agent's ticket and the API returns it. Sign-in worked correctly, but the request should still have been denied. Knowing who made a request and deciding what that person may access are separate boundaries.

Authentication establishes an identity using an approved mechanism, such as password verification followed by a session. Authorization applies the application's policy to that identity, the requested action, and the resource. A successful login does not imply permission to read every ticket in the database.

An opaque session token lets the browser refer to server-side session state without carrying the password on every request. The server validates the token and its expiration, then obtains the trusted user identity. Store the browser token in a suitably configured cookie; keep secrets out of application logs and avoid exposing the token to JavaScript when it is not needed there.

Cookie protections have different purposes. HttpOnly limits script access to the cookie. Secure restricts its transmission to secure connections. SameSite influences cross-site sending behavior. These properties support a session design but do not replace resource authorization, CSRF protection, or HTTPS configuration. The complete behavior must be checked in the deployed environment.

Sessions need explicit expiration and revocation. A logout should invalidate the relevant server session, and a password reset or deliberate sign-out-all operation should revoke existing sessions according to policy. Clearing only a visible user name in the browser does not revoke a token that remains valid on the server.

Use the server-established identity in downstream queries. A body field named ownerId is input controlled by the caller. It cannot establish who the caller is, even if the UI normally fills it correctly. The route should derive ownership from its trusted session context and apply policy before returning protected data.

Tests should distinguish no session, an expired session, a valid owner session, and a valid session for a different user. Each case asks a different question. A test that only checks the login screen cannot prove authorization, while a two-user resource test can expose a missing ownership predicate even when authentication itself is sound.
objectives: Distinguish authentication from resource authorization.
Explain the role and lifecycle of a server session.

Trusted user ID + requested ticket + action → authorization decision
~~~
The second decision remains necessary after the first succeeds.

items.title: Scope every resource operation
items.bodyMarkdown:
The ticket list correctly shows only the current owner's records, but the detail route fetches by ID alone. A user can bypass the list by requesting another ID directly. Authorization must follow the resource operation, not just the screen that normally leads to it.

A scoped query includes the trusted owner identity with the resource ID. Instead of reading any ticket with the supplied ID, it searches for a ticket with both that ID and the permitted owner. Under a consistent concealment policy, no matching accessible record produces the same 404 result whether the ID is missing or belongs to somebody else.

The policy also applies to writes. Editing, adding comments, and deleting or archiving a ticket must establish access before committing effects. A comment endpoint should not assume the parent was authorized because a browser previously loaded it. Every request is a new boundary, and another client can call the endpoint directly.

A pure policy helper can make a small rule easy to inspect. In this lesson, editing is allowed only when a user is authenticated, the user ID equals the ticket owner ID, and the ticket is not archived. This explicit rule avoids granting extra powers that the exercise never specified. More complex roles can be introduced when the domain requires them.

The helper does not remove the need for route integration. A correct function that no handler calls protects nothing. Test each endpoint through the real API with two fictional users and known owned records. Include the allowed owner's behavior so an overly broad denial is not mistaken for a successful repair.

For an unauthorized write, inspect the database afterward. A 404 response is insufficient if the handler already changed a row or added a comment before deciding what to return. Also inspect error details so no foreign title or comment text is disclosed. List responses must be scoped before pagination so foreign rows do not influence the visible page.

Keep the repair focused on the access boundary. A UI-only hidden button does not pass, and a framework rewrite is unnecessary when a missing predicate is the actual defect. The support-desk repair mission makes the flaw reproducible and asks for regression tests across detail, edit, comment, and list operations.

items.title: Protect requests and diagnostic data
items.bodyMarkdown:
A browser automatically includes a session cookie on eligible requests. That convenience is why the application can recognize the owner without asking for a password on every page. It also means a mutation endpoint must establish that the request came through an intended application interaction, not merely that a cookie arrived.

Cross-site request forgery exploits the browser's automatic credential behavior to induce unwanted actions. A session-bound CSRF token submitted through the application's request flow is one defense. Checking the exact expected Origin for state-changing requests adds another boundary. SameSite cookie settings help reduce cross-site sending but should fit the full design rather than serve as an unexplained single control.

Do not use GET for state-changing operations. Navigation, prefetching, and other browser behavior can issue reads in ways the user did not intend as a write. A read method should remain safe under the documented contract. Logout and content publication are explicit mutations with the relevant protections.

A CSRF token is not an authorization decision. A valid token says something about the request flow, while the authenticated identity and resource policy still determine whether the action is allowed. Similarly, CORS response headers are not a replacement for resource checks. Keep each defense tied to the boundary it actually protects.

Login behavior should avoid unnecessarily revealing whether an account exists. A generic invalid-credentials response and rate limits by account and source can make repeated guessing harder while keeping the flow understandable. Use established password hashing with appropriate parameters, and store no plaintext password. Administrative recovery needs a deliberate process because this private application has no public registration flow.

Logs must be useful without becoming another credential store. Record request IDs, route outcomes, timing, and safe error codes. Redact cookies, authorization headers, CSRF tokens, and passwords. Review the serialized log output, including failure paths, instead of assuming a logger setting covers every custom message.

Test wrong Origin, missing or invalid token, expired session, and repeated failed login attempts. Confirm that rejected requests change no protected rows and that logs do not contain submitted secrets. These tests complement ownership checks; passing one category does not establish the other. The resulting design should make both the accepted flow and its rejection behavior explicit.

items.title: Choose tests that distinguish wrong behavior
items.bodyMarkdown:
A page-count helper returns the wrong answer for partial pages, yet its test suite is green. The test computes its expected value using the same rounding expression as the implementation. Both contain the same mistake, so agreement does not establish correctness.

A useful test starts from an observable contract. If eleven records fit ten per page, two pages are needed. That concrete expected outcome can be stated independently of whether the implementation uses division, a loop, or another approach. Tests should preserve that freedom while rejecting behavior that violates the requirement.

Boundary cases make competing implementations disagree. For page size ten, totals zero, one, ten, and eleven distinguish an empty result, a partial first page, an exact page, and an overflow into a second page. A test using only twenty records would allow both floor and ceiling rounding to appear correct.

A regression test captures a demonstrated defect. Reproduce the failure with a focused input, write the expected behavior, confirm the old implementation fails, then apply the repair. If the test passed before the fix, it may not actually cover the defect. Keep the test close to the boundary where the behavior can be observed clearly.

Use the right test layer. A pure function test checks a calculation cheaply. A database integration test checks constraints, queries, and transaction outcomes. A component test checks how controls and state interact. A browser journey checks the assembled route and interface. More expensive tests should cover important integration boundaries rather than duplicate every small unit example.

Mocks let you control external outcomes, but they can also hide an incorrect contract. A mocked database that always accepts invalid references cannot prove a foreign key works. Use a real disposable PostgreSQL instance for the persistence rules the application relies on, and reserve mocks for external services or deliberately controlled UI timing.

Finally, test your tests with plausible wrong variants. An always-zero function, a floor-rounding function, or an input-mutating implementation may pass weak cases. Rejecting those variants is evidence that the suite distinguishes the intended behavior. It is not proof of every possible implementation, so keep the claim proportional to the cases and boundaries actually checked.
objectives: Select boundary and failure cases from a contract.
Critique tests that repeat the implementation.
commonMistakes: Calculating expected values with the same possibly wrong algorithm.

Using mocks as evidence that database constraints work.

items.title: Use diagnostics without exposing secrets
items.bodyMarkdown:
The owner reports that saving a note failed at 14:32. Hundreds of requests were processed around that time. A stable request identifier lets the response, application log, and relevant operation records point to the same event without requiring the log to contain the private note text.

Structured logs store named fields such as requestId, route, status, duration, and safe error code. These fields can be filtered and compared more reliably than a sentence assembled from arbitrary values. A request ID should follow the operation through the relevant layers so an operator can distinguish one failure from a nearby successful retry.

Choose log content deliberately. A complete request dump might contain cookies, passwords, CSRF tokens, repository URLs, or private learning notes. Redact credential-bearing headers and avoid logging bodies unless a specific safe subset is needed. Encoding a secret does not make it suitable for a log. Inspect serialized output from failure paths as part of verification.

Configuration also defines a boundary. Required values such as the database URL and application origin should be checked during startup. A missing value should produce a clear safe error naming the missing setting, without printing the contents of every environment variable. Failing early is easier to diagnose than an unrelated request error long after deployment.

Separate public configuration from server secrets. A frontend build can expose values embedded into its JavaScript bundle, so database credentials must never be passed as browser configuration. An environment example should document variable names and harmless sample values. The real environment file belongs outside version control.

Liveness and readiness answer different operational questions. A live process can respond while its database is unavailable. Readiness should reflect whether the service can handle the operations it promises, using a bounded dependency check. A health endpoint that always says ready can route users to an application that cannot persist their work.

Investigate failures by following evidence in order: which request failed, which boundary reported the error, which configuration or dependency was involved, and what changed recently? Keep the diagnosis specific. A missing DATABASE_URL requires a configuration repair, while a reachable database with a constraint violation requires a different investigation. Good logs make that distinction visible without retaining sensitive payloads.

items.title: Ship with a recovery path
items.bodyMarkdown:
A new application image starts successfully, but its note queries fail because the database migration was never applied. The container is running; the release is not usable. Shipping requires checking the contract between the image, configuration, schema, and real user journey.

Build from pinned dependencies and a reproducible source revision. Run type checks, static checks, relevant tests, and content validation before creating the release artifact. A successful build proves compilation and packaging, not that the deployed environment can authenticate or persist data. Keep those claims separate.

Rehearse migrations against an empty database and a representative prior state. Confirm the target application and any version that might be rolled back can use the resulting schema. Apply the planned migration at the documented stage of deployment, then check readiness and a small smoke journey through the actual service.

A smoke test should exercise a meaningful operation. Signing in, reading a lesson, saving a note, and reading it from another session verifies more than an HTTP 200 from the home page. Use appropriate disposable records for automated checks so verification does not overwrite real owner work.

Rollback has more than one meaning. Reverting to an earlier application image may be safe when the schema remains backward compatible. Restoring an older database backup replaces data with an earlier state and can discard legitimate writes made afterward. Do not call these interchangeable or restore data blindly to repair an application packaging error.

Backups need a retention policy, protected storage, and a restoration rehearsal. A dump command completing is useful, but a restored database with verified tables and records provides stronger evidence. Record the backup time, recovery procedure, and any expected data-loss window. Test the procedure before an incident forces you to depend on it.

When a release fails, stop making unrelated changes and collect the specific evidence: readiness response, migration status, safe logs, and the failing operation. Choose the smallest recovery that preserves valid data. Then add a regression or deployment check for the missed boundary and update the runbook. A clear recovery record helps the next change succeed without pretending that one successful deployment eliminates future operational risk.

Build and verify → inspect/rehearse migration → back up
Apply compatible migration → start candidate → readiness
Sign in → save disposable note → read from another session
If failed: inspect evidence and use the documented compatible recovery path
~~~
A running process is only one step in a usable release.

Calling the factory again creates another environment, so its count can evolve separately. Placing the count outside the factory instead makes it shared. A closure is useful for encapsulation, but its retained values still occupy memory while the function remains reachable. A finally block runs as control leaves the try/catch construct, so it is a useful place for cleanup needed after either outcome. Avoid returning from finally: that can replace the return value or error from the earlier block. Resource ownership should determine which layer performs cleanup; do not let two unrelated layers each assume the other will release it.

items.title: Model cancellation separately
items.bodyMarkdown: Leaving a screen can make its pending fetch unnecessary. An AbortController provides a signal that a supported operation can observe. A cancellation caused by navigation usually should not show the same message as an unexpected network failure. Create a fresh controller for each owned operation because an aborted signal remains aborted. Always retain a state-commit guard where work may still complete.

items.bodyMarkdown: A remote resource can be loading, successful, or failed. Independent optional fields allow impossible combinations such as loading with both data and an error. Keep transitions explicit so a previous error is not accidentally carried into a new success. The type describes permitted in-memory shapes; external JSON still needs runtime validation before it can be trusted as that union.

Scope overrides to your actual animated components instead of assuming every animation in the page has the same purpose.

items.title: Preserve a logical focus order

items.title: Validate at useful moments
items.bodyMarkdown: Showing an error before a user has typed can make a form feel broken. Choose validation timing according to the interaction: submission is a clear boundary, while field blur or later edits can help users correct an already identified issue. Browser constraints are useful but do not replace server validation. During async submission, prevent accidental duplicate requests and preserve a recoverable draft. A server rejection should map to the relevant field or form-level message rather than disappearing in a console log.
objectives: Apply validate at useful moments to a concrete implementation.
Diagnose and test the boundary: Clear the whole form after a rejected submission.
items.workedExampleMarkdown:
~~~text

If the count can be calculated from the current tasks, derive it during rendering. State should contain the minimal changing source values needed to reproduce the view. Expensive calculations may justify memoization after measurement, but duplicating state is not a performance strategy by itself. The same principle applies to filtered rows, selected labels, and whether a form can submit.

items.title: Use functional state updates
items.bodyMarkdown: State values in an event handler come from that render’s snapshot. Side effects such as requests belong outside the updater.

items.bodyMarkdown: Context passes a value through a component subtree without threading it through every intermediate component. items.title: Make retry an intentional action
items.bodyMarkdown: A retry is another attempt at an operation, not proof that it is safe to repeat. Read requests are often straightforward to retry, while writes may need a stable idempotency key or a status check. Preserve the original user intent and avoid silently duplicating effects. The UI should show when retry is pending and prevent uncontrolled overlapping attempts. After a successful retry, clear the obsolete error and display the acknowledged outcome. Errors should explain what the user can do next.

Failed read -> retry same query
Uncertain write -> reuse operation identity or check status
Confirmed success -> clear previous error

items.bodyMarkdown: Build responsive, accessible interfaces with deliberate React state and browser behavior.
items.description: Build responsive, accessible interfaces with deliberate React state and browser behavior.
targetOutcomes: CSS layout foundations: Understand box sizing, flexible rows, and resilient grids.
CSS responsive reading: Design for variable content, zoom, and motion preferences.
Accessible navigation and structure: Make pages understandable through landmarks, headings, and keyboard order.
Accessible forms and feedback: Connect errors, validation, and status messages to user actions.
React state architecture: Choose state ownership and keep derived values consistent.
React identity and reducers: Make reset behavior and multi-step interactions explicit.
Browser state and shareable views: Separate URL state, persisted preferences, and live page state.
Interface loading and recovery: Design honest empty, loading, error, and retry states.

items.bodyMarkdown: A URL identifies a resource while the request method communicates the operation. A read endpoint should not quietly perform a destructive action just because it is easy to trigger from a link. GET is intended for retrieval; writes require an appropriate write contract. Document which fields a write accepts and which effects it can produce so clients know how to retry and test it.

items.title: Use a stable pagination order
items.bodyMarkdown: A paginated query needs a deterministic ordering. If several records share a timestamp, ordering only by that timestamp can produce ambiguous page boundaries. Add a stable unique tie-breaker and encode the cursor according to that ordering. Keep filters consistent across pages, and reset pagination when the filter changes. Cursor pagination does not automatically provide a frozen snapshot of a changing dataset; define what concurrent inserts or edits mean for your list contract.

Diagnose and test the boundary: Order pages by a nonunique field without a tie-breaker.

ORDER BY created_at, id
-- Cursor comparisons must use the same ordered pair.
~~~

items.title: Make duplicate requests recognizable
items.bodyMarkdown: A client can lose the response to a write even when the server completed it. Retrying with a stable operation key lets the server recognize equivalent intent. Scope that key to the authenticated owner and operation, retain the result under a defined lifetime, and reject reuse with a different payload. The key alone does not provide atomicity; storing the operation record and applying its effect need a coordinated transaction or equivalent design. Tests must include concurrent duplicate attempts.
objectives: Apply make duplicate requests recognizable to a concrete implementation.
Diagnose and test the boundary: Reuse one idempotency key for unrelated payloads.
items.workedExampleMarkdown:
~~~text
owner + operation key + payload fingerprint
first request -> apply and retain result
equivalent retry -> return retained result
changed payload -> conflict
~~~

items.title: Detect stale writes with revisions
items.bodyMarkdown: Two tabs can load the same record and then save different changes. If both writes blindly overwrite the row, the second can erase the first without warning. Include an expected revision in the write and update only when it matches the current stored revision. Increment the revision atomically with the change. A mismatch should preserve the caller’s draft and return a conflict path. Deciding how to merge edits is a product rule, not something a version number can infer.
objectives: Apply detect stale writes with revisions to a concrete implementation.
Diagnose and test the boundary: Check the revision separately, then write without an atomic condition.
items.workedExampleMarkdown:
~~~text
Read revision 7
Update WHERE id = ? AND revision = 7
Set title and revision = 8 atomically
Zero updated rows -> conflict or unavailable record
~~~
commonMistakes: Check the revision separately, then write without an atomic condition.

items.title: Keep fixtures independent
items.bodyMarkdown: A test that mutates a shared fixture can influence later tests, creating order dependence. Construct fresh data for each test or use immutable fixtures with deliberate copies at mutation boundaries. Database tests need unique ownership or cleanup so one test cannot accidentally read another’s rows. Make clocks and random identifiers controllable when expectations depend on them. Isolation is not just cleanup after success; a failing test should not poison the next run.

items.title: Review the staged change
items.bodyMarkdown: The working tree, staging area, and last commit describe different snapshots. A commit records staged content, which may differ from the current file if more edits happened after staging. Review both status and the staged diff before committing. A clean diff is easier to reason about than a large collection of changes whose purpose is unclear.

items.title: Correlate logs with a request
items.bodyMarkdown: A user reports that one save failed while other saves worked. A request identifier can connect the browser-visible failure with server log entries without exposing the full private payload. Log the operation, outcome, duration, and relevant non-secret context. Avoid passwords, session tokens, and unnecessary draft contents. A log line saying only error occurred offers little diagnostic value, while logging everything creates privacy and operational problems. Use structured fields so related events can be searched consistently.

items.title: Engineering practice
items.bodyMarkdown: Make data contracts, tests, delivery, and production diagnosis part of everyday development.
items.description: Make data contracts, tests, delivery, and production diagnosis part of everyday development.
targetOutcomes: HTTP resource contracts: Define methods, response states, and representation boundaries.
API pagination and concurrency: Keep list traversal and repeated writes predictable.
SQL queries and relationships: Reason about joins, missing matches, and aggregate counts.
Database invariants and transactions: Protect relationships and multi-step changes under concurrency.
Behavioral testing and fixtures: Test observable contracts with discriminating examples.
Browser tests and async evidence: Verify interactions without brittle timing or selectors.
Git changes and release discipline: Make changes reviewable and verify the artifact that will run.
Performance diagnosis and operations: Measure bottlenecks, connect evidence, and prove recovery.

items.title: Build the support ticket interface
items.bodyMarkdown: Build a usable support queue from a React scaffold. Work with fictional tickets through the supplied mock API adapter, then prove the feature handles input, pending work, and failures.
setup: Unzip the starter into a new directory. Use Node 24.21.0 and pnpm 10.17.1.
acceptanceCriteria: Render the ticket list and a non-mutating status filter.
Require and trim the title; reject whitespace-only input with an associated field error.
Disable and guard duplicate submission while a delayed request is pending.
Show loading, empty, error, and confirmed success states.
Refresh the visible list after creation and retain the draft after failure.
Open a ticket detail through a route and display its comments.
Reach all controls with the keyboard and provide visible focus.
Keep the page within a 360px viewport; contain any exceptional overflow locally.
hints: Separate the local form draft from the server snapshot returned by the adapter. A list component can derive visible rows from the current filter.
Validate the trimmed title before calling create. Associate the error text with the input and use both a pending flag and an in-flight guard.
Await creation, invalidate the ticket query, and clear the form only after success. Pass the adapter through the feature so the later HTTP implementation can replace the mock.
items.solutionMarkdown:
[Download the M01 reference repository](/api/v1/assets/m01-reference-v6).

The reference separates the ticket list, creation form, and detail route. Form fields remain local state; server snapshots use query keys that include filters and cursors. A pure title validator rejects blank text before any call. An in-flight guard prevents duplicate requests, and the query is refreshed before success clears the draft. The shared adapter lets M02 replace fixture calls with HTTP without rewriting the feature. Run both baseline and mission checks and inspect the delayed-response regression.
reflectionRubric: Explain which values belong in local form state versus server state.
Describe the whitespace and delayed-response cases and why the tests distinguish the defect.
Record keyboard and 360px observations, including any remaining limitations.

items.title: Extend the persistent ticket API
items.bodyMarkdown: Connect the completed interface to a Node.js API and PostgreSQL. Implement validated ticket creation, deterministic pages, details, updates, and comments. The fictional identity header is a training fixture; production authentication is outside this starter.
setup: Unzip the starter and read its README. Use Node 24.21.0, pnpm 10.17.1, and Docker Compose or a local PostgreSQL service.
Copy .env.example to .env, then docker compose up -d db.
pnpm db:seed — run twice to check repeatability.
pnpm dev:api — in another terminal run pnpm dev.
baselineChecks: pnpm test:baseline — requires the migrated training database.
acceptanceCriteria: Validate title and body before creating rows; trim the title and reject unknown input fields.
List tickets with bounded page size and deterministic createdAt/id ordering.
Return a cursor that preserves the complete page position and avoids duplicate IDs in the documented fixture.
Return 404 for an unavailable detail record.
Require an existing accessible ticket before creating a nonblank comment.
Ensure invalid input and rejected comment requests change no rows.
Apply migrations to an empty database and run the seed repeatedly without duplicates.
Connect the HTTP adapter and show useful API errors while preserving form input.
Pass database tests covering empty data, multiple pages, tied timestamps, and missing records.
Inspect generated SQL and explain the foreign key and transaction boundaries.
verificationCommands: Create and migrate a separate support_desk_test database as documented in the starter README.
Set DATABASE_URL and TEST_DATABASE_URL to that same disposable *_test database.
With the training API running and VITE_API_MODE=http: pnpm test:e2e
hints: Keep the route responsible for parsing and response mapping, and use the provided Prisma schema for durable relationships. Complete input validation before starting writes.
For pagination, order by createdAt then id, fetch limit plus one, and encode both fields from the final returned row into the next cursor.

For comments, look up the accessible parent inside the operation boundary, return the consistent unavailable response when absent, then create the child. Test the rejected path by checking row counts afterward.
items.solutionMarkdown:
[Download the M02 reference repository](/api/v1/assets/m02-reference-v6).

The reference uses strict runtime schemas at route boundaries, owner-scoped queries, and a composite cursor ordered by createdAt and id. Comment creation checks the parent before writing inside a transaction; PostgreSQL independently enforces the foreign key. The frontend HTTP adapter translates API errors into the same contract as the mock adapter. TypeScript describes validated values but does not validate remote JSON by itself. Run the disposable database suite and inspect the emitted SQL in a local fictional-data environment.
reflectionRubric: Explain which invariants belong in request validation and which belong in database constraints.
Explain how tied timestamps are handled across pages.
Describe why a rejected comment creates no row and where the transaction begins and ends.

items.title: Repair the ownership boundary
items.bodyMarkdown: Investigate a runnable support desk with Alex and Morgan as fictional users. The starter intentionally fetches tickets without the required owner scope. Reproduce the flaw through API tests, repair the shared boundary, and prove allowed owner behavior remains intact.
setup: Unzip into a separate directory so the intentional defect remains isolated.
Copy .env.example to .env and start the documented PostgreSQL service.
pnpm dev:api — fictional identities use X-Training-User: alex or morgan.
baselineChecks: pnpm test:baseline — verifies service readiness and fixtures, not ownership correctness.
acceptanceCriteria: Alex cannot read Morgan’s ticket through the detail endpoint.
Alex cannot edit or comment on Morgan’s ticket, and denied writes change no data.
List queries apply owner scope before pagination.
Unavailable and inaccessible resources consistently use the documented 404 policy.
Error responses contain no foreign title, body, or comment details.
The legitimate owner can still list, read, edit, and comment.
Regression tests cover every affected endpoint and verify persisted effects.
Responses and logs retain safe request correlation without sensitive content.
verificationCommands: Configure and migrate the separate *_test database described in the README.
Run pnpm test:mission before the repair and record the cross-user failures.
Repair the owner boundary, then run pnpm test:mission again.
hints: Begin at the direct API request: the list UI cannot authorize a separately issued detail or comment call. Trace how the trusted fictional identity reaches each query.
Inspect ownedWhere in api/policy.ts. Every list, detail, edit, and comment lookup should constrain the resource by ownerId.
Return a predicate containing the trusted ownerId and, when supplied, the ticket ID. Keep the existing 404 response behavior and rerun both denied-user and allowed-owner cases.
items.solutionMarkdown:
[Download the M03 reference repository](/api/v1/assets/m03-reference-v6).

The focused repair returns {ownerId, ...(id ? {id} : {})} from the shared owner predicate. Routes already use that boundary for list, detail, update, and comment operations. Tests verify 404 responses, absence of foreign content, unchanged rows after denied writes, and successful owner operations. A hidden UI control would not pass because the tests call the API directly. The identity header remains an explicitly fictional training mechanism, not production authentication.
reflectionRubric: Write the defect explanation in terms of the missing server-side resource boundary.
Explain how each regression would have caught the original issue.
Describe why a 404 response alone is insufficient without checking that no write occurred.
